entry.title: Weekly Notes 39/2026
entry.content:
In one of my earlier blog posts, I mentioned that I have become more routine, more protective of my time, and indirectly more productive since becoming a parent. That continues. I totally get how Parvathy feels in this video. I am still not a proper morning person. I wake up around 6 AM. That said, I pay close attention to how I feel physically and mentally, and I also pay close attention to rest. Most of my awake time goes into what needs immediate attention and being nice to my future self.

This week has been tough but interesting overall. Lots of good conversations, both technical and non-technical. I hope to find more time to write next week.

  • Uma wanted to get on a digger; she asked me. I said I don’t own it; if you want, you need to ask driver uncle. She called him loudly and asked him if she could come inside. He said, “Yes.” After a while, she asked, ” Can you start and move the hand? He said, “No.” I was just watching the conversation.
  • This week’s P.T. was at odd times because I was traveling; thanks to Bhumika for accommodating. I couldn’t play this week, but I was able to run wherever I was, which is a good thing.
  • The Indian Express has done a good series on the CEC and ECI of India. For me, the most worrying factor was that technology blocked what the law allowed; hence, 97 voters couldn’t be added to the voter list, and I think it’s a crime that should be punishable. Also, what was decentralized in process and pre-tech is now centralized by technology; i.e., voter list creation is decentralized but centralized technically, and storage and RBAC are centralized. Ideally, each state should own the platform with a separate installation and database. They should sync to the central one only for reporting purposes, as it used to work before. We are kind of losing it due to the centralized architecture design, and it goes directly against the Constitution.
  • I was in Chennai to meet the team. It was a very short but hectic trip. I couldn’t get a train ticket, so I took a private electric bus. I must say KSRTC (Karnataka) has the best buses in the country.
  • I like that Anand includes “Mistakes I made” and “Questions I was asked” in his weekly updates. Lume is a small, crazy-fast hybrid search engine written in Rust; you can run it locally or on your server.

entry.title: Unclenched Cramping, it works?
entry.content:
I had my periods this week.

I don’t have an internal clock or tracking, so they often arrive as visiting guests: “Oh we were visiting your friends in the neighborhood, and it’s been a month since I have seen you so here we are!”

On the night before my periods, I was reading an article [1] on Substack about unclenching. And I have long known clenching to be my default state. Eighty percent of my waking time, I am clenched, the article was a reminder and how it affects our body, I read half of it and fell asleep.

I woke up the next day with period cramps and decided to apply the article? And I am weirded out by it, that it worked?! I personally cramp a lot on my first day of periods, they are the worst and I hate them. They can be painfully debilitating at times. So I lied down and consciously relaxed my body and put my hand on my stomach, the self-touch was gentle, warm and caring and when the cramp came instead of fighting it internally, I let it through and it felt better. But when I was not paying attention I’d reflexively fight back the cramp making it worse, so it took me some time to relax and let it wash over me. It was good in a weird way.

Since the first day was a huge success and I was “filled” with weird wholesome feelings, next day I decided to work! And that backfired, as I was sitting on my desk and looking at the nvim code, I started to cramp real bad, I realised that while working I had started clenching again, which aggravated the cramps. I took a break and focussed once more on relaxing, which helped.

I was using a heat pad on the side, I have macho-ed through this for the past twenty-seven years of my life, I am gonna provide whatever help I can to my body.

My first experience of unclenching, I’d like to think of it as full body relaxing, was when I came back from Vipassana, my chest-support straps kept falling off my shoulders, which was weird because they could not all have worn out at the same time. I realised that my shoulders were relaxed, and the size of the strap was adjusted for tensed up state.

I know how weird it is say, but I had a good run of periods this time. Touchwood! I am planning to repeat this experiment and post an update.

Cheers,
Calra

P.S. a mini-rant (Note: this bit was added later in the article)
I hate how the period adverts when I was growing up were mostly around, wear these magical pads with wings and play all the sports, it is not impossible, but trust me, it’s very physically taxing especially in the first two days.  The body is still doing the hardwork, think if there were an advertisement for fever going like, “hey wear this icepack for fever and go play football!” the body is still exhausted, you can still play football but it is not recommended, it’s an exaggeration, I get it, but you must understand where I am coming from. I am sure, the original ads were trying to fight against the older traditions and taboos of “keeping women (read it as people who menstruate)  indoors”, reminds me of a line from A Room of One’s Own by Virginia Woolf, either women are treated as divine or inferior, protected, never just human. Sad.

[1] How to Unclench

entry.title: Tracking execution events for your WorkManager Workers
entry.content:
WorkManager is Android Jetpack’s first party solution to long-running background work. It takes care of dealing with the idiosyncrasies and differences between Android versions, and gives you a very simple API that lets you focus on what needs to happen instead of the how. It’s very well designed, and as someone who’s had to deal with JobScheduler and AlarmManager years ago for this class of problems, it’s a boon.

That said, debugging WorkManager is somewhat cumbersome (ref). This also had the limitation that it only lets you debug issues on your own device, and collecting metrics from the field required instrumenting each worker manually to report back metrics which just doesn’t scale all that well.

Enter: ExecutionEventListener. This is a brand new API that was introduced in WorkManager 2.12.0. The WorkManager team has also introduced a new work-analytics library on top of this low-level API to retrieve historical execution data, but we’ll focus on ExecutionEventListener. It is still experimental, so you’ll need to mark your code with @ExperimentalEventsApi.

As of writing, the API looks like this:

You start by creating a subclass of this interface, then pass it to your WorkManager Configuration.Builder like so:

I wired this up in my app Claw to emit events to Sentry, and can now visualize them via a dashboard to see data like failure rates and p50/p95 of execution duration. Here’s the relatively minimal dashboard I set up which has collected a couple of days of data through my internal testing channel.

Naturally with this still being a new API, there are some quirks to it. The major one is that while you get a ListenableWorker.Result instance in the method parameters, all three subtypes (Success, Failure, and Retry) are marked with @RestrictTo(RestrictTo.LIBRARY_GROUP) which means Lint flags any attempt to use them for determining what the result actually is. I’ve filed an issue to provide a solution for this. In the meantime, you can simply suppress the Lint like I do. Another problem is the lack of support for @IntDef and friends in Kotlin, which means the stopReason parameter arrives as a plain Int. When publishing this as a metric, you’ll have to check its values against the WorkInfo.STOP_REASON_* constants yourself and map it to a string.

You can find my implementation here which deals with both these paper cuts.

entry.title: Waxing poetic about my records and turntable
entry.content:
Music in the streaming age is weightless. It reaches you through the aether from servers thousands of miles away into whatever speaker happens to be nearby. It seems almost infinite, is completely free of friction, and incredibly easy to take for granted.

I recently bought a record player and my first three records, with plans to buy more.

To anyone used to tapping a glass screen to hear any song ever recorded, this looks like too much work to listen to a limited number of tunes. Records are bulky, inconvenient, require physical storage, and only hold about twenty minutes of music per side before you have to get up and flip them over.

Yet, much like taking the time to manually grind whole coffee beans instead of stirring instant powder into boiling water, the friction adds to its appeal.

The instant coffee vs. freshly brewed coffee analogy breaks down when it comes to quality though. Any coffee connoisseur will say brewed coffee tastes better than instant (due to a variety of reasons), but standard CD-quality digital audio technically has higher fidelity and dynamic range than vinyl ever will. Records degrade over time due to dust and scratches, leading to sound artifacts (which I am coming to terms with), and cost a ridiculous amount of money in India, thanks to import duties and a weak rupee.

What makes a record “worth it”, still

I’m sort of a minimalist and never thought I’d have a collection of anything, but I love music and hate how exploitative streaming is (more on this later), so it makes complete sense to have a little record collection.

Here are some reasons I started one, in no particular order.

Difference from digital media

Unlike digital files which store sound as a collection of bits, a vinyl record is a direct physical artifact of audio.

When a record is pressed, soundwaves are literally etched into a single continuous groove on a sheet of PVC plastic. If you zoomed in with a microscope, you'd see the actual undulating shape of the soundwaves themselves.

It’s such a delicate, magical, yet simple thing, and it boggles my mind that this exists at all.

Relative rarity

Vinyl records went out of fashion because of their cost of production, fragility, and low portability, and everyone streams, so it makes the experience even more interesting, as I didn’t get to listen to any until recently. You did however see them in all sorts of media, especially that from the heyday of records, which added to the mystique.

The art looks really pretty

The sleeve, of course, has the album art, which is usually pretty enough on its own, but they also quite commonly have things like lyrics booklets,

Records themselves look good as well

Our first record, “Ali” by Vieux Farka Touré and Khruangbin, was a translucent blue-green instead of the usual black, which was such a pleasant surprise.

Another record I purchased, “Is This It” by The Strokes, is a limited editiion translucent red.

Plain black records also look great, though.

You might enjoy the music more

The ritual of pulling the disc from its sleeve, gently lowering the tonearm, and watching it spin anchors your attention to the room. It turns listening into a dedicated activity rather than background noise.

Dust and cat hair gets on the record, which causes pop sounds, and the act of moving it to and from the sleeves and the turntable creates static, which makes a sort of buzzing sound. This means you have to clean a record each time to get the debris out and remove the static. You really have to love a record to want to go through all of that. It connects you to the activity of listening instead of being a passive participant, and I guess the work makes you appreciate it more?

Streaming pays very little

The artist gets more money. If you buy a record in India, maybe 10% of the sale price has actually gone to the artist (because the retailer, the government, the publisher, etc all take their cut), but it takes 100,000 to 150,000 streams on Spotify for an artist to net the same amount. Streaming is hell for smaller artists especially, and is not enough to make a living.

A section of Wikipedia on Spotify’s compensation practices

More miscellaneous reasons

  • My partner’s cousins and brother have one.
  • It’s a physical display of your music tastes.
  • Actually owning your music.
  • Records and the turntable and other equipment look really good in a room, and you can talk about it.

Neighbourhood record store

I live quite close to this cute record store called On the jungle floor. They’ve got a massive collection of records and the staff is friendly. I love visiting there to just look at the really expensive equipment they have and drool at the LPs they have.

Two of the records we’ve bought have been from here!

An interesting thing I heard after a couple of conversations there with people either working or hanging out there as friends of the owner, people volunteer there for free for some reason? Not sure why anyone would do that other than as a favour to a friend. If any reader has done something like this for a for-profit business, please let me know.

There was a guy behind the counter who wasn’t an empployee. He’s a DJ and was playing some of his personal records from a massive tote bag full of records, trying to figure out what to play on his next set. Maybe he was getting the most out of the ₹3L turntable. I didn’t get to talk to him too much, but my partner really liked the LPs he had, and since we can’t find them for sale anywhere in India, this has caused a lot of consternation. For anyone who wants to check out his music, his name is Saksham, @ghewxr on Instagram.

The current rig

I’m using an almost entry-level turntable from https://www.headphonezone.in/, the AT-LP60X. It doesn’t have a lot you can mess with, for instance, it does not have an adjustable counterweight on the tonearm (the part that holds the needle), which means one less thing to mess with and mess up, in my opinion.

I just use a portable bluetooth speaker via aux at the moment because dumping all my disposable income into a new hobby would be silly. Even when I do get speakers, I’m going for the (relatively) cheaper end for now. I’m not an audiophile, and thank god for that. Like every hobby there’s a way to dump all your money into this. After a certain point, you get diminishing returns and are just trying to optimise the fun out of your equipment.

I’m thinking of doing listening parties, though, and the idea of bringing people over to listen to music coming out of a cheap portable speaker does seem a bit sad. Down the line, the goal is to set up a proper stereo amplifier connected to a decent pair of passive bookshelf speakers, preventing the speakers from turning the record’s stereo sound into mono, add more depth to the music, and fill my room. The bass on the Strokes album goes hard, so a subwoofer is also on the cards.

Thinking of getting the Polk Audio Monitor XT15 Speaker from avstore.in alongside the Fosi Audio V3 amplifier. This will go great with my HiBy music player as well (because of the aux input), letting me listen to digital music from a more “intentional” source than streaming from my phone.

entry.title: (#2026-W38) maps, comics, birbal and stickers
entry.content:
On Sunday, the chronicles of the long weekend continued. I went to the Museum of Art and Photography with Sumnima, where we went through the an exhibition called “A Moving Line: 1500 Years of Indian Visual Storytelling”. ¶

Now, don’t kill me, but this was my first time going to MAP after being in Bengaluru for four years. I probably have many Reels and links of this place saved, of exhibitions that have long come by and gone. MAP to me is one of those must-go places here, and so I was glad to finally do my MAP darshan with Sumi. ¶

I also want to mention that I really appreciate the accessibility of the whole place. A wheelchair ramp for the entrance, a lift big enough for even a motorized wheelchair to enter comfortably, and self-opening doors with key cards placed at a comfortable height. The staff was really helpful and friendly too. The place is well thought through. ¶

The exhibition itself was wonderful. We were in a quiet room with red walls, surrounded by artwork drawn over multiple decades. Historical prints existed in the same space as modern Indian creators, with even showcases of the adoption of language in visual art across the country. ¶

The part that I loved the most is the inclusion of Amar Chitra Katha. Growing up, I can’t remember a single comic I read that wasn’t under ACK’s umbrella of work — except maybe Chacha Chaudhary from Diamond Comics, who was a travel partner on every train ride. The cartoons and their stories always lingered in my memory. ¶

But yeah, the exhibition had a complete wall of covers of ACK’s comics, including ones of Mahabharata, Lord Krishna’s Chronicles, and Akbar & Birbal. Man I love Birbal. Birbal is the coolest. They also had a vinyl of Birbal’s stories. Did I tell you I love Birbal? ¶

There was also this little leaflet in the centre of the exhibition, where you could complete a comic strip by drawing your own story. I drew from an epiphany that left me and Sumi laughing for a long time. You can ask me for it if we meet in person. ;) ¶

I don’t particularly remember how the Monday went by for me. I remember seeing a lot of my Marathi friends posting Stories from their Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations and I sent a mental prayer to all the pictures of idols too. ¶

I also undertook the surgical process of increasing the storage of my main partition on my laptop. I say “surgical” because I learned that the laptop makes a familiar beep every second when in recovery mode, similar to those patient monitors in hospitals. Not to say that they are the same thing, ofcourse. I feel like I have to disclose that stuff nowadays. The resizing was ultimately a success. ¶

Saturday was spent hanging out with the folks at IndieWebClub. The meetup this week was more development-related and set around digital housekeeping. I started out with the intention to work on my Nannoo’s website, but I quickly got absorbed in talking to many of the other attendees about their set tasks instead. ¶

I’ve sort of developed an appreciation for the ways in which people have come to use LLM’s. The technology itself is still as crude and intellectual theft-y as it has ever been, but these humans have come to utilize it in a way that brings their warmest ideas to life. ¶

Divjot recently shifted his Now page to look more like Orkut, while Arpit made a portal for the his wife’s monthly Bengali meal service. Jatan, who isn’t a programmer by profession, jailbroke his Kindle and fine-tuned his calm writing setup with help from LLM’s. I have some apps that I am working on myself, with the intention to ultimately spend less time on my devices. ¶

I don’t know, we might be able to abstract our way out of our technological pit and get back to our human connections. But there’s a lot of fascism to be cleaned up before we get there. ¶

That’s all the musing there is this week! I am getting very sleepy now. Sweet dreams, dear reader. ¶

entry.title: Water on the Moon and Chandrayaan the first, collaboratively catalyzing a global lunar rush
entry.content:
17 years ago this week, a paper published in Science announced the discovery of water on the Moon by India’s Chandrayaan 1 orbiter. Changing the notion of a bone-dry Moon as cemented during the Apollo era, the finding had fundamental implications for understanding the origin and evolution of our Earth and its cosmic companion. That water was present on Luna in multiple forms also meant it could be used as a resource for future deep space exploration, offering breathable air for astronauts, water to drink and use, and fuel when its hydrogen and oxygen is liquefied to power longer, more ambitious missions. This potential, combined with the Moon’s proximity making it a technological catalyst, has led to nations around the world sending or planning to send a flurry of robotic and even crewed missions to the Moon. Chandrayaan 1 catalyzed a global Moon rush after the decline of last century’s Cold War lunar race at the dawn of the Space Age.

The discovery of lunar water came through a notable act of collaboration. Chandrayaan 1 carried 11 scientific instruments, six of which involved foreign partnerships across five nations. Lunar water’s presence was confirmed by the Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3) instrument onboard Chandrayaan 1, provided by the US’ premier space agency National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Some other Chandrayaan 1 instruments also saw signs of water but M3’s detection was the unequivocal one. It could differentiate between ice, liquid water, and water vapor based on how the lunar surface reflected and absorbed infrared light, which meant avoiding false positives in measurements. M3 was also an excellent mineral mapper; its data has helped scientists worldwide churn out hundreds of lunar findings and counting. Noah Petro, a former Project Scientist for NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) mission and currently a Science Lead in the agency’s Artemis program to return humans to the Moon, praised M3 in 2019:

10 years ago today Chandrayaan-1 ended. I was so lucky to be a small part of that mission. The M3 instrument allowed us to take a huge step forward in learning about the composition of our 8th continent!

Unlike countries with developed space programs, India had not been one to explore worlds in our Solar System other than Earth for most of its space-faring life since the 1960s. With Chandrayaan 1’s launch in 2008 on a PSLV-XL rocket, India forayed into planetary exploration. Confirming water’s presence on the Moon was a primary mission objective for the Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO), the country’s governmental space agency who designed, developed, launched, and operated Chandrayaan 1. That India achieved such an important discovery & goal on its debut planetary mission inspired people around the world, including myself. I was in school at the time, fascinated by all things space and science. Chandrayaan 1’s water gem catapulted my imagination of the international prowess of space exploration. It’s worth remembering that collaboration is what catalyzed Chandrayaan 1’s success.

Late Srinivasa Hegde, who worked at ISRO’s Satellite Center for 36 years, was the Mission Director of Chandrayaan 1. Hegde was deeply involved in many aspects of the mission: the design of the various mission phases, data management, orbit determination, strategies for course corrections, orbiter operations, and so on. I asked him during a 2020 interview about the driving philosophy behind ISRO soliciting scientific instruments from other space agencies around the world for Chandrayaan 1. He noted the following:

We had our own science payloads on Chandrayaan 1 but we also wanted to provide the spacecraft as a platform for others we could collaborate with. And so ISRO put out an announcement of opportunity to scientists all over the world to pitch payloads for Chandrayaan 1. We got instruments from ESA as well as NASA, including universities associated with them. I think the timing of Chandrayaan 1 was good as NASA’s next Moon mapper LRO was still a year away.

Past missions had hinted at water’s presence on the Moon. Because of its potential for exploration and future economics, space agencies globally were keen to confirm water’s presence. NASA responded to ISRO’s call for payloads and got to fly two of its water-hunting instruments onboard Chandrayaan 1: the M3 and the Miniature Synthetic Aperture Radar (Mini-SAR). The latter found indications of water ice in more than 40 craters host to frigid permanently shadowed regions on the Moon’s poles. But just like with efforts in the previous decade such as from NASA’s Clementine lunar-mapping orbiter, the data wasn’t conclusive by itself to rule out false positives, such as certain rough rock textures mimicking water-ice-like signals. M3’s measurements provided independent proof of water’s existence, and validation for some measurements by other instruments.

Among the many more scientific results that came out of Chandrayaan 1, another collaboration stands out. India, Sweden, and the European Space Agency (ESA) collaborated on the Sub-keV Atom Reflecting Analyzer (SARA) instrument. By analyzing how protons—hydrogen nuclei—in the Sun’s radiation wind impact the Moon and get reflected, SARA helped scientists better estimate the amount and distribution of water or hydroxyl molecules locked in the soil across the Moon. The discovery helped future confirmation of water’s presence across the lunar globe, embedded in its soil and rocks. It also proved timely for ESA’s ongoing BepiColombo mission to study Mercury, which carries instruments similar to Chandrayaan 1 for detecting water.

Operating and balancing the goals of 11 instruments on Chandrayaan 1 as a debut planetary mission wasn’t easy. One of Hegde’s tasks was to accommodate the needs of foreign instruments onboard alongside optimal craft operations. In his own words:

It posed challenges because they [the foreign payloads] had diverse requirements. For instance, scientists behind Mini-SAR wanted to calibrate the instrument when the spacecraft would be en-route to the Moon. They were unhappy with the fact that we couldn’t accommodate that due to certain changes in our launch schedule. However, at a later stage we provided them with a geometry in lunar orbit for calibration which they said was even better than what they originally asked for.

Following up on Chandrayaan 1’s findings, missions from China, USA, India itself, South Korea, Europe, Japan, and more are trying to unravel the exact nature, state, and abundance of lunar water as the next logical step. Sustained crewed lunar exploration plans by China and the US also depend on it.

Related: Interviewing Chandrayaan 1’s Mission Director

The Indian Government’s Department of Space (DOS), under which ISRO operates, stated the cost of the Chandrayaan 1 mission to be ₹386 crores in 2008, which is approximately $89 million in 2026. As far as lunar and planetary missions go, that’s on the lower side of expenditure. As evident by the debut mission’s fundamental discoveries, welcoming foreign instruments proved effective in increasing mission science without increasing costs. Participating nations got to fly their scientific instruments without having to build an entire mission of their own. At the same time, experience gained by ISRO in developing and/or operating some planetary instruments in collaboration with NASA and ESA helped the agency make fully indigenous, state-of-the-art instruments for the Chandrayaan 2 orbiter.

For Chandrayaan 1, India also established the Indian Deep Space Network to communicate with the spacecraft as well as future planetary missions. The mission established operational experience for India with spacecraft at the Moon, feeding into future planetary missions. Hegde noted here that the India-US partnership on Chandrayaan 1 also extended to NASA providing ISRO with access to its iconic Deep Space Network. It was used for communicating with Chandrayaan 1 for additional bandwidth, and when the craft was outside the range of India’s newly built planetary communications network. This deal with NASA for having additional communications layers for ISRO’s planetary craft has persisted through India’s first Mars orbiter Mangalyaan, the Chandrayaan 2 orbiter, and the Chandrayaan 3 landing mission.

The world is now mounting numerous Moon missions. As we directly explore the treacherous lunar south pole and its water, we would be wise to remember the compounding effects of collaboration and sharing to make expensive, high-frequency exploration not only safer and more successful but also efficient. Chandrayaan 1’s catalyzing of a global Moon rush can remind us of the collaborative mindset the world needs more of, if only we remember its vantage point.

entry.title: Use date trees to organize chronological notes in Obsidian
entry.content:
I recently built Date Trees, an Obsidian plugin to help me better organize my journal entries and daily notes. You can download it from the Obsidian plugin directory, or read the rest of this post to understand why I built it.

Note

I built this plugin almost entirely using coding agents. I reviewed every line of generated code, and often rewrote parts of it when it wasn't up to snuff. I also added an excess of comments to the code to ensure I understood it completely (a post for another day). I'm comfortable taking responsibility for this work.

However, I'm including this disclaimer here because I don't feel comfortable taking credit for something that was largely built by a machine.

Taking responsibility but not credit. What does that say about our current moment in tech?

I've enjoyed journaling for as long as I can remember. In high school and college, I wrote in spiral-bound notebooks with cheap blue ballpoint pens. Eventually, as a young adult, I switched to writing in plain Markdown files on my computer.

These days I begin most mornings with a fresh cup of coffee and a Markdown file whose filename is the day's date in ISO 8601 format (e.g. 2026-09-21.md). I then shut off all distractions and write about a thousand words, or until my mind is empty of thought. I started this practice in 2014, journaling intermittently whenever I felt like it. In recent years, it's a rare day when I miss my morning journaling hour.

In the twelve years since I started journaling digitally, I've accumulated nearly a thousand Markdown files (I counted). The ISO 8601 format for filenames ensures all files are automatically sorted in chronological order when I view the folder in my file manager or the Obsidian sidebar (as long as my sort order is set to filename). Like this:

- Journal/
  - 2014-03-13.md
  - 2014-03-14.md
  - 2014-03-15.md
  - 2014-03-16.md
  - ...
  - 2026-04-01.md
  - 2026-04-02.md
  - 2026-04-03.md
  - 2026-04-04.md

But, as you can imagine, navigating a folder with a thousand files (and counting) is not easy, even when they're sorted chronologically. There's no hierarchy of any kind to help me digest the collection in smaller chunks.

It's easy enough to pull up an entry for a specific date—you just type the date into a search box—but casually browsing through the archive or navigating quickly to a specific month in a specific year using a pointing device is not a comfortable experience. A giant list of files is also difficult to navigate on mobile.

To make these entries easier to navigate, I eventually reorganized my journal so the files were tucked into folders and subfolders using a sensible hierarchy. Something like this:

- Journal/
  - 2024/
  - 2025/
  - 2026/
    - 01/
    - 02/
    - 03/
    - 04/
      - 2026-04-01.md
      - 2026-04-02.md
      - 2026-04-03.md
      - 2026-04-04.md

With this hierarchy in place, if I wanted to figure out what I was doing on 21 September 2016, I could go to the folder for the year 2016, then the ninth month, and then scan the relatively small number of files for the correct date. And the notes still automatically sorted themselves into chronological order at each level of the hierarchy. Much better!

This is how I organized my journal, daily notes, and other chronological notes for several years. Until I discovered something better.

Many moons ago, during my brief time using Org Mode to make sense of my life, I came across the idea of a date tree. From the Org Mode documentation:

You generally use date trees within Org files to organize your notes into chronological sections. The package includes shortcuts to help you create these hierarchies, move them around, visualize them on a calendar, quickly capture notes into them, and generally slice-and-dice them in an Emacsian manner.

I didn't care about organizing individual files as date trees. My Markdown files rarely contained notes for more than a single day. But I realized I could use date trees to organize a folder structure. This is what it looks like:

- Journal/
  - 2024/
  - 2025/
  - 2026/
    - 01 January/
    - 02 February/
    - 03 March/
    - 04 April/
      - 2026-04-01 Wednesday.md
      - 2026-04-02 Thursday.md
      - 2026-04-03 Friday.md
      - 2026-04-04 Saturday.md

This has all the benefits of my previous system: an obvious hierarchy and automatic chronological sorting in most file managers and notes apps. But adding month and weekday names to folder and file names makes navigation even easier. This organization strategy doesn't require me to constantly map month names to month numbers and back, which usually takes me a bit of cognitive effort. Further, having the name of the weekday in the filename makes it easy for me to "see" full weeks in my file manager, and also helps me guess at the contents of the file.

Date trees are now my default method for organizing chronological notes and other files across my computer. Depending on the volume of files I need to store, I can omit one or more levels of the hierarchy. And, as an additional bonus, it's easy to write scripts to parse these folder structures in order to process or automatically reorganize them. Which is exactly what my plugin does.

Of course, you can create these date tree structures manually in your file manager or notes app. But if you use Obsidian, my plugin makes the process a little easier. It lets you right-click folders in your vault to mark them as date trees.

You can then use the command palette to quickly create new daily notes or open existing ones.

The plugin also lets you assign a template to each date tree (though the template implementation is an ugly hack at the moment). In the future, I'm planning to add the ability to navigate backward and forward chronologically within a date tree, and to open every historical entry from the same calendar date.

I've been using this plugin for three months. By now I have several date trees set up in my vault, including:

  • My personal journal (the initial use case)
  • Daily notes
  • Devlogs for programming projects
  • Therapy notes
  • Ongoing notes for long-form writing projects

If you are one of the seven people in the world who care about folder structures as much as I do, please try out my plugin. If you'd like to give me feedback, file bug reports, or contribute new features, you can do so on the project's GitHub page. You can also write to me via email.

I hope Date Trees can help you tame your own ballooning notes folder.

entry.title: Weeknote September 15 - September 20 2026
entry.content:
This week has been kind of low as well. But for reasons which are so stupid and probably relatable that I had to blog about it.

I want to introduce the phrase "Sweet Little Hope" based on "Sweet Little Treat" which Gen Z has adopted as a way to cope with the weird way this economy and world at large is headed.

I realised that in the doldrums of unemployment, I am not actually worried about getting a job because a getting employed is a foregone conclusion. What I am worried about these days is finding some kind of companionship.

The truth is that we live very lonely, fragmented and isolated lives. I am watching people have comforts which I am dreaming about. They are enjoying the performance of success and happiness, crying about their dreams coming true.

This feeling of being left behind in a quagmire comes from watching the simulacra of fictional people who are basically characters in a endless stage play I can scroll past. Everyone in instagram is a theatre kid at heart hoping for a big break, but once in a while that illusion shatters and I am left feeling sad and empty.

A couple of months ago a child who was opening Pokemon card packs was served on my feed. Avery was excited, but i could see it was forced. He had terminal cancer.

Making these videos gave him some comfort because I could see genuine excitement break through whenever he pulled cards which were valuable according to him.

I don't understand the speculative markets that the pokemon card industry has been taken over by, but I recognise and respect that Avery got a lot of joy and comfort from sharing this hobby with the world.

Over the weekend he was admitted into hospice and he is dead now.

This might seem like a convoluted and parasocial eulogy to a boy I barely knew but sometimes it's easy to see yourself reflected in the people you glance at.

I'm glad that he got his youtube play button before his passing and I am glad that the community he formed and the wider pokemon card community has rallied around him and his parents.

So when I say "Sweet Little Hope" I am trying to convey this idea that it's not a crime to look forward to doing small things which might seem silly to other people. As an adult it becomes increasingly difficult to make connections because people become jaded but if you could do even a small act of kindness even if it is for yourself you should do it.

I know it's pedantic to say "take joy in the little things", but maybe it's basic stuff like this we tend to put in boxes along with all the messed up trama that happens just by existing.

I have had to come to some conclusions about what direction I am headed. It seems inevitable that the people who were here for most of my life will become less pronounced now. Some people whom I thought would be around forever are long gone completely. It's a lonely thing watching people leave.

So my sweet little hope is working on finding my kind of people, it doesn't have to be permanent because ultimately the truth is all relationships have a natural expiration date one way or another. So I'll take joy in my attempts of reaching out, because one must imagine me happy.

entry.title: Can I just say that everything sucks?
entry.content:
I was talking to my peers, and every single one of them currently feels anxious, uncertain and insecure about the future. Some are impacted by a layoff, some are anticipating one, some settled for a pay cut, while others are figuring out ways to make money to fund their life or parenthood. My nephew himself is concerned about which career to pick, as white-collar jobs seem to be dead ends or easily replaceable. I mean, what sort of world have we created that education is being undervalued? Is this made up? Is my internet wrong? Is it just my threatened privilege feeling concerned about its general expectation of "life will get better" not adding up anymore?

I really don't know how to make my point without qualifying that, of course, education is a privilege in a third world country, having a white collar job at all, let alone from pre covid era is a privilege, not having job insecurity for even few years is a privilege. What I really want to say is that, even that privilege is seemingly eroding away.

🔗suppose

Say you are indeed laid off today, not because you underperformed, but because a clanker has been trained by learning (read stealing) from millions of people like you who involuntarily built the knowledge base for it. What do you do now? Do keep in mind that you would now be competing for a job with many other senior and junior candidates, thus driving the value of your cognitive abilities further down.

🔗jester-ification of education

Perhaps you become a content creator. You package a skill, an opinion, a hobby, or a private moment into something that can hold attention long enough to be monetised. It was even a genuine route taken by one of the impacted folks in this video.

To be clear, I don’t think content creation is lesser work, nor do I think social and cognitive skills are opposites. I’m unsettled by the possibility that more and more people may have to turn themselves into a product to survive. Attention becomes job security; personality becomes inventory.

The platforms reward urgency, spectacle, parasocial intimacy, and persuasion. Even people who begin by making useful, thoughtful work can be nudged towards constant performance and conversion. The fear is not that people make art, teach online, or build communities. It is that precarious work might push everyone into the same competition: perform, persuade, monetise, and keep performing or disappear. In fact, the entire loop is to use these advertising platforms to target demographics to sell more ads to. They collect data, you sell ads. Which demographies are more likely to buy from you? Vulnerable ones? Addictive ones? Hopeless ones? What things are more likely to be sold? Ones that make their lives genuinely better? Ones that make this world a less anxious place?

I call this jesterification of education: not because creators are jesters, but because a system that promised stability through learning may now ask people to entertain the market to remain economically visible.

I read a post from a dear member of Indie Web Club after writing this post, and I wholeheartedly agree with the facts they were sharing. And, I also feel grief over losing out on the promise of education. Can I just say, this sucks?

I don't know what the endgame here is if all desk jobs are to be replaced with an "agent". I am pretty sure the mission statement of these AI companies ultimately is to replicate the output of a group of humans who set out to solve a problem. But if white-collar workers are not paid, who pays those who depend on the income of white-collar workers? Who is all this in service to? Is it simply late-stage capitalism, baby?

🔗systemic failure

Much of my angst is also coming from feeling abandoned due to the failure of democracy and corporations in providing law, order, stability and jobs. I mean, I live in a country that proclaims to be the mother of democracy, while actively curbing dissent. It is almost like it treats its own citizens as cockroaches.

You can't walk for more than 100 meters in any city of this country no, really, any city, without seeing garbage, inhaling the pollution, hearing excessive honking, playing the game of Subway Surfers IRL while walking on a nonexistent footpath, or feeling the free rollercoaster ride one gets by driving over potholes on frequently dug-up roads, all while sensing a lack of empathy for fellow citizens.

🔗scarcity

On empathy, I see a deep sense of scarcity in many people around me, especially in urban India. Much of it could simply be fabricated, but I am pretty sure their feelings driving it are very real. Why shouldn't they? Many have experienced generational poverty or insecurity at some point, and even if their parents had what would seem like a relatively rich life by today's standards, a paid-off house in their 30s, a cute hatchback car, two or more kids, and a long career at the same company ahead of them, with a pension, which they reluctantly had to retire from; there was, and still is, scarcity behind it all. One may even argue that this very scarcity mindset prevented lifestyle inflation back then, it was a survival mechanism.

But today, that same mechanism can make us see every person as a target to outpace, a seat in public transport to be "stolen" from a fellow passenger, and an inch of gap in traffic as a campsite until the next inch opens up. Of course, we feel entitled to these things because our problems were much worse than others, and now the world has to pay back by adjusting to our needs. We are always in a rush, never pausing to reflect on whether we are trading today's peace for a hypothetical peace in the future. Can anyone convince me that tomorrow will surely be better than today? If not, then why should I rush my way to worse tomorrow?

On one hand, we have more food than ever, more clothes than ever, cheaper renewables, and more money (in the hands of very few) than ever. Yet it feels like there is immense scarcity amid an abundance that remains unreachable. With education failing to provide stable employment, are we really carrying this scarcity mindset into a much bleaker future? I shudder to imagine what that world would look like.

🔗get out

I am not the only one to rant online about systemic failures. It isn't hard to find comments like "Leave this country ASAP" or "Don't return back you'll regret it" online. Maybe these woes are indeed solved elsewhere. It isn't hard to find citizens of country I reside in being surprised by how easily they are able to walk over 20K steps abroad, or how traffic could clear without a single honk. But then, it's not like the citizens of the countries my fellow citizens are fleeing to have a very positive outlook on life themselves, regardless of their political leanings. Housing crises or cost-of-living crises are just terms now; they don't even feel like "crises" that require "urgent" solutions. Yet, there are unemployment cheques, public schools are functional, there are more green spaces, and governments are trying to aid new parents.

It feels so tragic that I feel I literally have to uproot my life in pursuit of a more humane experience. In fact, for my community specifically, I feel generationally displaced, with no "village or hometown" of my own, each generation leaving one country at a time. I may someday write a bit more about that. I wonder what would my hypothetical self from a better country write today, would he have the same experience too? How much of this is wrong place and wrong time? How much of this is simply, wrong person?

🔗wait, was Karl right?

When I read about Karl Marx's concept of alienation, it looks like I'm simply describing symptoms of alienation. Even if he saw it coming, what have we done about it? What are we doing about it?

I'll ask again, is my internet wrong? Can you convince me that this is all in my head and life is actually beautiful? What kool-aid langar did I miss out on? Do I have the wrong personality? Am I just feeling the loss of community and third spaces, because the point of life is not avoiding pain, but experiencing it with others? Whom am I asking this of? Are you listening? Do you feel this too?

  • my very slow and reflective reading of Anxiety by Samir Chopra
  • two drafts that got merged into this rant
  • this video about layoffs
  • this video about how to have fun even if it is bad for you

  • this video about a driver trying to vlog simultaneously to make ends meet, and they seem successful on both accounts, so kudos to them!

This is not Udaipur, it's a random building in some random narrow street in Surat.

Life

Michami Dukkdam

Michhami Dukkdam to everyone 🙏

In short: If I have wronged you in any way, please forgive me as do I

In long: This is something all the Jains say to each other after completing the Samvatsari Pratikaman, which is considered most important ritual of the year. After 8 days of intense spiritual activities, it is also expected to some extent that a devotee ruminates about all the wrong doings they might have done to a particular person. You usually start with the list of people closest to you, most of the times that's family. Then you move on to friends, colleagues, etc. etc. At the end of the stick are the people you meet occasionally, who you might have wronged unintentionally. I really like this philosophy of Jainism, if followed properly, it forces one to introspect deeply about yourself and your relationship with others.

This might sound similar to the yearly review you do to get your salary hike and in a way it is! Just like it, you don't start thinking about your achievements once in an year. You do that and there is a higher chance to miss out something important. Same is the case with this, its encouraged to make it a part of your daily life. It's a form of daily journalling I believe? Whatever it is, I really like the idea of it. Hopefully someday I can incorporate it at a deeper level :).

Hilarious replies to Michhami Dukkdam

  • This is where you be humble for a day and go back to being a dick from tomorrow? This is the Gujju equivalent of oil companies saying they're terribly sorry for oil spills and drilling for oil the very next day.
  • is this just an excuse to be a menace all year and then throw this once to cleanse yourself like the white girls pouring water over their heads
  • is it rude if i say no as a joke
  • Not to be freaky but what if we hugged until we both felt okay again

Chauviyar Upvas

After my Tela (3 days of fasting), I did another fast on Samvatsari. But this time, I notched it up a little by not drinking ANY water for the whole day. I had been doing this ever since I was a kid, but had stopped in recent years cause I used to do Tela at the end of the Paryushan, and third day of fast without water with SO MANY activities is like hell! But as I had completed the Tela early this time, I got a nice chance to sneak in one more fast :).

Paushad

On Samvatsari every year, I take Paushad. This means living the life of a Jain saint for a day. It's like Nayak but with saints in it xD. And yes, there are people who like the life so much that they decide to walk the path of saints for the rest of their life. Now last day of Paryushan i.e. Samvatsari, has a LOT OF activities itself. Add to them all the strict rituals you follow for living a cheap imitation of saint life, it's a HELL. I leave my house around 04:00 in the morning and return back home after 22:00, at which point I am so exhausted I can't do anything except falling on my cozy bed and sleep like a baby. This is made worse by the fact that I usually have my third fast day or Chauviyar Upvas that day. You get zero downtime between these hours, and also don't have any luxuries of mobiles, etc to use. A daily of pure spirituality. It's a bliss. A lot of people, also take Maun (not speaking anything for the whole day). Everyone has their own ways of getting more "spiritual". I have been doing it for the last 15 years and hope to continue doing the same for the rest of my life :).

Night out

Just the very next day, me and Sanyam went out to check progress on the house he is building and also grab some tasty Rajasthan dinner at a new place we wanted to try. My FAFO originated with both of us roaming around trying all the different food places in Surat xD.

She and I are family friends and have been hanging out with each other ever since we were born (literally!). We went around doing Pandal hopping as it was Ganesh Chaturti. I clicked a LOT OF PHOTOS! Coco is like chocolate milk but 1000x better, sorry I know I am kinda butchering a drink I love so much, but trust me, if you ever end up in Surat, you gotta try this!

entry.title: Let some doors be squeaky
entry.content:
Author’s Note: I briefly talk about a trans friend’s experience of body dysphoria and body image.

Hello,

this is a response post to some comments made about squeaky doors in the IWCB whatsapp group chat and the use of WD-40.

Dear WD-40 user,

The harbinger of silence, of smooth hinge movements, I put forward my counter-case. I like some doors squeaky, they give the consistent feedback of opening [1] and then closing again. And that feedback is a vital signal to the brain to close the loop. I invite you to a thought experiment, imagine applying WD40 to your knuckles, so next time when you crack them, they don’t pop, how would you feel? Wouldn’t you feel slightly less satisfied? Sure, the stretch back and forth was tension relieving but the final satisfaction, you will miss that. You will feel un-whole. That something that yours was taken away from you and you are given something which the society deems polite. It reminds me of my college friend before she knew she was trans, she went through a liposuction surgery to get her man-breasts removed for her to have a “normal” social life, but instead of feeling euphoria and feeling more like herself, she felt worse, she felt something that was hers was taken away from her only because society thought it looked weird and others felt uncomfortable by it and her parents were trying their best to help their child. Sad. Tragic. Ain’t it?

Next, you go on about applying WD40, please ask the people, if they are even really bothered by it? Or rather is it the last sound of their day, of that quiet squeak of the door they hear closing and know they are safe now.

Yours dorkly,
Calra

entry.title: Thirty seconds at a time
entry.content:
I am losing my attention span (and taste)

It’s 9:30 at night, and I open Instagram instead of reading the book in my hand. The first thing that pops up on my screen is a 30-second reel. It is a scene from the movie Hidden Figures.

You probably know the scene. Taraji P. Henson, playing mathematician Katherine Johnson, runs across the NASA campus in the rain to use the “coloured” bathroom. When her boss finally asks where she disappears to every day, she gives him a truth he was not ready to hear.

I think about the humiliation Johnson and so many others faced, the anger they must have felt, and the defiance it took to continue doing their work. I feel riled up every time I see it. It makes me appreciate the film, the performances and the lives of the people it is based on.

There is just one problem. I have never watched Hidden Figures.

Well, let me correct that. I have “seen” it. I have not watched it.

My Instagram algorithm has evolved into a different beast over the past few months. As I have tried to spend less time on the app, it has found newer, more devious ways to suck me back in.

And it is succeeding. I often find myself watching movies in 30-second instalments (sometimes television shows too). A dramatic confrontation. A clever chase scene. A powerful courtroom speech. A final act of revenge. Then another clip, and another, and another.

Sometimes I see so many clips from the same film that I can piece together the entire plot. I know the characters, the conflict and how it ends. I can appreciate the story and discuss its best scenes (not that I ever would).

This has become my primary relationship with Instagram.

Credit where it is due to whoever is clipping and packaging these stories, whether it is a person or an AI tool. The edits are remarkably effective. They give me just enough context to care, then end at exactly the point that makes it impossible not to watch the next clip.

Sometimes I open the comments and find bots talking to other bots, posting the same empty reactions. Somewhere among them, there will be a comment asking, “@grok, what movie is this?” Yep, even on Instagram.

That is usually the moment the spell breaks. That one comment gives me enough of an ick that I want to throw my phone away. At least until the next time I open the app.

Being addicted to short videos is a problem in itself, but what frustrates me more is the habit displaced by this mindless endeavour.

I barely watch movies anymore and have seen only two in theatres over the past six years!

It sucks to admit that because I used to love going to the cinema. In college, I would watch as many as three movies a week, often by myself. I bunked numerous classes and failed a few exams, but I always made it to the theatre.

Now, even watching a movie at home feels difficult. The opening credits have barely begun before I feel the urge to reach for my phone and check another notification. Or even better, watch a 30-second clip of another movie while the one in front of me is about to start.

A two-hour story feels like a commitment, while Instagram guarantees shots of 30-second emotional highs on demand.

I don’t know exactly where I am going with this blog post. Maybe I needed to say this out loud and let go of some of the shame around it.

Maybe I also need help. Definitely need recommendations!

Recommendations on how to get past this addiction, and recommendations for good films. I like warm films, action films and animated films.

I promise to watch them for longer than 30 seconds. And when I finish, I’ll share my thoughts with you.

ideas · personal · culture

entry.title: Walking Like An Assassin
entry.content:
This is not a how-to post. it is but a silent admission of the status quo of how I live my life.

I walk like an assassin — with minimal noise. There are many things I do to make my existence small and invisible, I think this is one of them and has spooked enough people by now that I thought to address it in a blogpost. I have had trouble sleeping at night and I often had the need to get up to pee or drink water. And my mum has been sensitive to sounds, lights and noises, so when at home, if I need to move around the night, I imagine myself to be Tom tiptoeing around the Spike’s doghouse. It’s funny and sad.

I have often walked up to friends in the kitchen and made an inane comment or remark, like, “oh this is how you chop the brinjal” and they have often been startled or gulped down a “Whoaa”. With one friend, it happened so often, we agreed on me doing comms around and calling from far “hey…I coming to the kitchen”. The only reference I have for such explicit communication is from Flatland by Edwin Abbot, where women have to keep on declaring their presence and position with a sort of Peace-cry. More context on that, all women are straight lines and look like a point from another direction, so it’s easy to get hurt or killed. So they have a separate entrance and and have to keep talking all day.

One of the side effects, of this invisibleness is, people often tend to step on my toes because they don’t realise I am right behind them. No, I didn’t sneak up on them, I just walked up to them, deep sighs. And then I am dealing with second order effects of keeping enough distance between the person I walked up to, it is tragic honestly. If I were to wave and greet, and make my presence known, it’d be much easier.

I don’t recommend doing it but if you ever end up being in position like this, your partner or friend is sick and you don’t want to disturb their sleep, here are some reference pointers:

  • if jumping, always land on your toes, it makes less noise.
  • when getting up from bed or cot, especially if it creaks, get up laterally, by that I mean don’t put the entire pressure on a single point. If it’s a low floor bed, I just roll off the bed on all fours. And then stand on the floor.
  • if you are lying back down in the bed, it’s the same try sliding in laterally, there’s less depression formed and won’t alarm the sleeping person.

Ciao,
Calra

entry.title: The media and arbitrary ethics
entry.content:
Sometime back, someone from a legacy Indian media outlet called me and asked to write an article on Indian space within five days, and for free. They expected me to agree to commit to it then and there itself. I said I’d have considered contributing but the timeline is too short and I have other things to do so I’ll pass. They insisted again, as if it’s a demand for some reason. I said okay, the short timeline could work if you republish one of my articles from my blog. They vehemently said no, calling it to be an ethical issue.

Wait, what?!

Of all the shady and questionable practices that media outlets follow, such as ingesting notorious amounts of ads, intentionally avoiding or stripping off attribution links for information sources, not naming the research paper being covered, normalizing delayed payments, and so on, where they draw an arbitrary line is republishing an article? That too in the name of unspecified ethics?

How on Earth is republishing an article with a linkback to the original with the author’s permission an ethical issue? Outlets republish stories often, and my articles have been republished with credit by The Space Review, The Planetary Society, The Wire Science, and more outlets. So why do many other outlets like the one that called me have an issue with such an arrangement especially when they’re the ones expecting writers to do the work for them, to meet their time demands, and do it for free?

Because many media outlets operate so opaquely on multiple fronts, and legacy publications especially think they’re above all, people have lost trust in the media, and are instead more than happy to believe social media influencers. 🤦🏻‍♂️

entry.title: correct reply to a young person who asked me for career advice ((it's true))
entry.content:
[someone emailed me. question redacted. this answer is lightly edited for presentation.]

This is going to sound blunt—but everything in the industry is changing. And so is everything in the world.

I'll let you in on an opinion I hold that I haven't talked about with a lot of people very much, because it sounds a bit obtuse, but I sincerely think this will help you.

The idea of "career" and "work" is fundamentally fake. They are neat constructs and boxes drawn by modern industrial society. There used to not always be jobs, and the idea of a "career" is still younger (barely a few hundred years old). We just happen to fall in a blip in history where we created one box that bundles in the idea of income, daily structure, socialising, status/purpose, and the expectation of a ladder of rising seniority into this thing we call "work." Everyone's life revolves around work, which we created a boundary for, which means we now have to define another fake boundary called "leisure" and then have to figure out how to do "work-life balance." Even if they are recognised in our laws and economy, they are fake and arbitrary boundaries of convenience. Think about it: do we talk about chore-life balance? Entertainment-life balance? Exercise-life balance? There is only life, and there is nothing to balance.

This bundling of various things we do in life into packaged jobs will go away. Powerful AI will unbundle them and dissolve most normal jobs as it diffuses through the economy. In a way, it has already killed a certain class of junior engineering that used to exist in my time, it's just not diffused yet. It has already eaten up a big chunk of what I used to do, and I think there's maybe a good 5-10 years (in the best case) after which it will be generally better than me at all the things I know to do today. But I'm not too worried, for reasons I'll outline soon (editor's note: reasons were not clearly outlined).

What I'm trying to tell you is that you are aspiring for a future of a specific shape that will not exist. Think broader, bigger and more long-term. Almost no one does this, because it's uncomfortable to do so, and so they pick the "default config" that life offers to them. What you should seek is not an "appropriate workplace" or WLB. What is worth pursuing is a well-examined, good life. Start with the outcomes and work backwards from there to see what will support those outcomes. Apply the hacker mindset there, see that the idea of "work"/WLB/"succumbing to a workplace"/"being compensated fairly" are mere abstractions, ones which are falling apart.

Let's take an example: say you have lots of hobbies, you want a life where you can pursue a whole bunch of varied hobbies/passions, but you also need to earn a living. You can work at an "easy" but maybe not so technically demanding/low status job where you get lots of free time to pursue these passions (think Kafka working in insurance, or Ted Chiang being a software documentation writer). The other end of the spectrum is doing demanding, fun work—maybe you want to make your hobby/passion as your source of income, and it might be something that will demand most of your time, and something where it doesn't matter whether you have "work-life balance" because it's just weird to think of a thing you are having a blast with in those terms. Most startup founders would fall into this category.

It's also too early for you to settle on a specific line of work, especially when the world is not going to be the same or recognisable anymore in 10 years. Again, do you want to work in a domain, or do you just want a well-examined, fulfilling life?

The only thing that will matter soon enough is the capacity to autonomously set goals for yourself, be willing to pursue those goals, and see reality clearly enough that you know how to manipulate it. So what do you actually want deep in your bones? No human is born wanting to one day become "a fairly compensated labourer with work-life balance." These are all artificial concepts of a modern industrial society. See through it and figure out what it is underlying all of this that you actually want.

entry.title: Non-negotiables in My Digital Personal Space
entry.content:
I wrote this post for a prompt given during our local Indieweb club meeting: “Write about non-negotiables in your personal space.”

My MacBook Pro is my digital personal space on which I spend hours every day. Absence of some particular tools and capabilities is a deal breaker for me now, even if I switch to a different laptop or OS.

First, I require a tiling window manager to use anything at all on my laptop. I don’t want to bother with moving windows around, fixing overlaps, changing their sizes etc. The window manager should do these for me and should be drivable by keyboard shortcuts. Currently I use Amethyst on macOS.

Next, I want to configure my machine programmatically instead of going around tweaking hundreds of knobs. Not only is it cumbersome, but fairly non-reproducible too. Another reason I want this is to be able to easily move my configurations over time to newer machines I get. Currently I use nix-darwin and home-manager for this purpose.

Since I write a lot of text (code and prose), a fast editor is indispensable for me. It has to be configurable too, because I like to adapt it to my liking. The editor for code should support popular programming languages and color schemes. Currently I use Zed and Bear.

A fast editor must be accompanied by a fast terminal. Again, it needs to have good configurability, but I generally don’t require many external plugins. I mostly use default layouts, and do not require scriptability. Currently I use Ghostty.

Dark mode support is must have for all applications I use. In 2026, if your app doesn’t support dark mode, I’ll drag it to the trash bin without batting a single eyelash.

I spend a lot of time looking at code, so I like having nice looking and highly legible monospace fonts. My current favourites are Pragmata Pro, Fira Mono and Jetbrains Mono.

As a programmer, I use CLI tools all the time. So I definitely value them enough to get to know them and make informed choices. I like my tools to be fast, feature-full, easy to learn, and composable with other tools. I list many of the tools I use in this post I wrote a few years ago: Software I use on my MacBook.

I may be forgetting a few more, but I think this covers the most important ones.

entry.title: A Cantonment Road
entry.content:
There’s a place I go to in my head sometimes. An empty, curving road. It has those blinking red lights running along its center, the way roads in Army Cantonments have. I can also feel I’m in an Army Cantt., though I can’t tell which one. It could be Shankar Vihar or Jalandhar or anywhere else. The streetlamps are those old ones with bulbous heads, except the yellow halogen lamps have been switched out for cold, white ones. ¶

The place is stuck in nighttime. You can hear all the different bugs you usually do on a cold night like this, with only grass (or maybe trees) on either side of the road. I can imagine myself wearing my thin white windcheater, standing on the road. I never move, never walk. I just watch the road and the lamp and the blinking lights. ¶

I can’t see it, but I can feel that my house is nearby. Maybe on the other side of the curve. I imagine the Army quarters painted in white and my cozy warm room nested in there. I can imagine those yellow lamps old Army houses had outside, ones with a metal grid in front of the glass for a reason that I never figured out. ¶

This place has remained permanent for a few years inside my constantly moving brain. But I’m yet to know if this is me being nostalgic towards something I have experienced before, or a yearning for somewhere I wish to be. I can’t tell if it’s a glimpse from my past or my future. All I can feel for it is yearning. I miss it in a way. ¶

I sometimes wonder – out of fear – if I’m actually seeing the place where I will die. I am standing in the middle of the road after all. I have never thought about vehicles in this place, but maybe that’s the oversight that costs me my life. But it’s too morose to taint that nostalgic place with fear, so I just continue to leave it to its mystery. ¶

This place I’m unsure of continues to stay in my heart. And I go stand in that place from time to time; maybe because standing alone there feels better than standing alone here. ¶

entry.title: When every service becomes an accountable transaction
Brief experience report on the DeepSeek v4 Flash model
entry.content:
NOTE

This is not going to be exhaustive, I didn’t compare them against exactly identical tasks, and this blog post is effectively me turning a somewhat wordy journal entry into a short blog post. Take it with an appropriate amount of salt as per your dietary needs.

I’ve recently been testing out the famous Matt Pocock skills package to rebuild a slop tool that had achieved slop singularity and become such a mess not even the clankers could figure it out any more. I’ll probably write a separate thing about that process (early hint: I get why it has 260K stars) but this post is mostly about the swap from Codex to DeepSeek. For access to DeepSeek models, I signed up for OpenRouter and paid them $10 for an initial top-up of credits.

I had already built around 70-80% of factual-budget with Codex (last pre-DeepSeek commit is this), and swapped to DeepSeek to implement the final feature of writing out transactions to Actual Budget. I haven’t figured out how to share the session transcript in Pi’s nice HTML format yet, but 🔜™️

Here are my main takeaways so far

  • DeepSeek models are thinkers. I initially set up DeepSeek with the high reasoning effort I use with other models but the reasoning going on for aeons started ticking me off and I switched reasoning to off. This might not exactly hold true, but since OpenAI redacts thinking traces for Codex users, I might just be overly sensitive to the LLM reasoning word vomit.
  • They seem extremely averse to tool calls. Maybe it’s something with Pi or my specific setup? The LLM consistently chooses to invoke cat, sed, and find when my system prompt includes specific guidance to use the harness-provided tools instead of shelling out. OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s models do not exhibit this problem in my experience, and Kimi seems to share this drawback with DeepSeek.
  • The inference speeds were comparable to OpenAI at the start of the session, but were much more unstable as the session reached around the 150K token mark. I think that is an OpenRouter-specific problem because it can send every request to a different provider and cause prompt cache misses. I was able to extract a per-provider split for my current measly $1.75 spend and that backs the theory.
  • The token pricing is simply unreal. I used OpenRouter’s simulation feature to compare my DeepSeek cost with what it would be on other frontier models and the difference is stark. For very comparable code quality it is a no-brainer to prefer DeepSeek over everything else.

All things considered I’m quite impressed with the DeepSeek models, and I can see why OpenAI and Anthropic seem to have found common ground against open weight models from China when they’re so close in capabilities. So far it doesn’t seem any such regulation is coming, and I hope for other countries to also step up and start competing in the open weight division instead of buying into the Anthropic and OpenAI silos.

entry.title: (#2026-W37) writing, coding, reading, repeat!
entry.content:
After an eventful week previously, I spent this week chilling and finishing up work tasks. With that out of the way, let me make a tangent. ¶

I recently read this post by Harsh, where I was drawn specifically to this quote in reference to Artifical Intelligence: ¶

Tech has spent decades automating away everyone else’s job, it’s poetic that we eventually do it to ourselves.

And since I read this, I have been noticing the word “automation” being repeated in conference rooms and stand-ups more and more. To a degree the automations are necessary; with the speed of work and the volume of results increasing, there is a need for scripting to handle chunks of the workload. But a lot of that problem is created by the fact that the floodgates of this technology are currently wide open. ¶

I also notice that people use future tense a lot when referring to AI in a sentence. AI will replace complex roles completely. AI will do all the work and we won’t need people anymore. AI will replace you, so you need to learn everything as soon as possible to keep up. I wonder if we’re just making promises to ourselves and running desperately to achieve them. ¶

Ever since the last IndieWebClub meetup, I have felt an urge to finish up the rest of my drafts and publish them. The progress has felt great, but I realized most of them were stuck because my own feelings on the topics were unresolved. Figuring that out is tiring. :P ¶

Sooo I’ve been working on that. I wrote a continuation on my double thank-yous, but also decided to write fiction in the moment on Saturday. To anyone who’s interested in reading that, you might like to learn about “The Holy Trinity” in Hindu mythology for context. ¶

For the technical people who might be interested, I recently started dabbling in Sätteri plugins for Astro. I used to use Remark/Rehype for post-processing on my markdown files, but since Astro shifted their default processor (and since Sätteri is written in Rust), I decided to port over the plugins I used to Sätteri. I now have one for processing image captions and one for auto-linking paragraphs. ¶

I’m also currently working on this app called “Graycie”, which is supposed to help me manage grayscale mode (and soon, night light) for each app instead of just a system-wide toggle. I’ve wanted this for a long time because – as much as I love keeping the phone in black-and-white – I still like taking pictures, looking at pictures, and doing video calls in colour. ¶

Manually toggling the mode is cumbersome, so I’m working on developing (mostly agentically) and releasing this on F-Droid. That itself is taking a long time though, as you can see in this merge request. But this was definitely a productive week programming-wise. ¶

I ended the week with having dinner at my aunt’s and spending time with the family. A lot of time spent on VSCode and GitHub/GitLab this week, and staring at screens overall. Maybe I’ll try going out more in the next week. ¶

Alright, I’ll see you around. Peace and love. ¶
